name: Retro-Futurism / 70s Sci-Fi
era: 1968-1982 (models), revived as a design language since about 2012
origin: The look comes from three films and one typeface family. In 1962 Aldo Novarese drew Eurostile for Nebiolo -- the extension of Microgramma, designed in 1952 by Alessandro Butti and himself -- with its squarish, corner-rounded letters modeled exactly on the shape of a television screen. Kubrick's '2001' (1968), Ridley Scott's 'Alien' (1979, production design by Ron Cobb and Moebius among others) and 'Blade Runner' (1982, Syd Mead) made it the standard typeface of the future. Because real computer graphics were unaffordable at the time, the screens were built from film loops, amber and phosphor-green CRTs and labeled plastic panels -- the technical constraint produced the style. Exactly that materiality, later christened 'Cassette Futurism', is what gets quoted today: a future that still has toggle switches, cassettes and scan lines.
idea: The future as used industrial equipment: an interface is a labeled machine with a housing, a channel number and hazard stripes -- not a floating surface but a thing somebody works on.
markers: Chamfered corners instead of radius: a 20px clip-path chamfer, always on diagonally opposite corners (top left / bottom right)
Amber #FFB000 and phosphor green #57E06A as the only signal colors on housing brown-black #14120C
Wide squarish sans in caps with 0.06-0.16em tracking (the Eurostile/Michroma line), never for body text
Technical labeling as a mandatory element: channel, system and counter labels in 10-11px monospace
26px tile grid, visible as 4.5% amber lines on the screen ground
Corner brackets (2px thick, 16px long) as a substitute for a frame -- the screen has no continuous edge, only two diagonally opposite brackets
Hazard stripes at 45 degrees, 9px pitch, yellow #E8B400 on black, as the closing edge of the housing
Scanlines 1px/3px at 30% black plus a radial CRT vignette from 52% radius outward
Keys with a hard 4px plinth shadow with no blur (0 4px 0) that drops to 0 when pressed

params.radius: 0-3px on surfaces, 12px only on keys; corners are chamfered by 20px instead
params.depth: no soft shadows: depth comes from housing-within-housing staging, 1px chamfer edges, inset black on the screen and hard plinth shadows on the keys
params.color: Two phosphor colors (amber, green) as the complete vocabulary on warm black -- amber carries structure and action, green carries operating states only; yellow appears in the hazard stripe alone
params.type: Wide squarish sans in caps for titles, names and key labels, monospace for everything measurable -- times, counters, channels; no third family
params.motion: Mechanical rather than soft: steps(1) blinking at 1.1s (cursor) and 2.4s (LED), a linear scanline sweep at 6.5s; state changes 120-180ms linear
params.texture: CRT: scanlines 30%, vignette, 4.5% tile grid, plus a traveling brightness sweep at 5.5% opacity

examples.name: Alien (1979) -- the Nostromo bridge and MU/TH/UR
examples.what: Amber CRTs with scan lines, Microgramma labels on every switch panel, hazard stripes along the edges, screens sunk into massive plastic housings

examples.name: 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968)
examples.what: Eurostile Bold Extended as the labeling typeface throughout, tile grids of rectangular readouts, displays set flush into wall surfaces

examples.name: Blade Runner (1982), Syd Mead
examples.what: The Esper machine and the Spinner cockpit: green-and-amber line displays with crosshair overlays, art deco edges, visible wear on the housings

examples.name: Alien: Isolation (2014, Creative Assembly)
examples.what: Fully diegetic UI: flickering CRT terminals, chunky keyboards, amber menus -- the most rigorous modern implementation, played deliberately as a technical constraint

examples.name: Signalis (2022) and the Teenage Engineering OP-1
examples.what: Phosphor-green low-res readouts with monospace labels, and hardware with channel numbers, chamfered edges and a warning color -- the evidence that the language carries as a product outside film too

strengths: The only one of the three nostalgia styles with high contrast out of the box: amber #FFB000 on #0E0C08 sits at roughly 11:1
Very information-dense -- technical labels, counters and channel numbers are part of the style rather than ballast, which suits dashboards and monitoring tools
Fully tokenizable: a chamfer angle, two signal colors, one tracking value, two type families -- it mirrors into Compose and SwiftUI with nothing lost
Corner brackets work as focus and selection markers instead of being mere decoration
Ages more slowly than Y2K or Vaporwave, because it points at a closed film iconography rather than a consumer trend
risks: Tips into costume fast: as soon as the technical labels are invented rather than real (channel numbers that number nothing), the whole thing looks like a game menu
Amber on black is strenuous over hours -- the color glows hard and tires the eye far sooner on long text than white on dark gray
There is no credible light mode: phosphor needs darkness, and a light variant is a complete redesign
Wide caps eat horizontal space and break onto a second line immediately with long compound words (and on mobile)
Scanlines and vignette are either invisible or a moire problem on low-resolution or brightly calibrated displays
a11y: Contrary to the cliche, this is the most accessible of the three: amber on warm black reaches roughly 11:1, phosphor green roughly 10:1, all body text sits well above 4.5:1 and the 1px scanline layer costs only about 10% of that. The real problems lie elsewhere -- the wide caps sans measurably lowers reading speed and is therefore limited here to titles, names and key labels, while times and counters are set in monospace; amber and green are hard to separate for deuteranopia, which is why status is additionally coded through dot shape (round = active, square = paused) and border style (solid/dashed). Blinking LED, cursor and scanline sweep are switched off under prefers-reduced-motion, and no animation falls between 3 and 50 Hz.
longevity: Because the style comes from a closed, canonized film iconography rather than a consumer trend, it ages more like a genre than like a fashion -- 'Alien' did not look more dated in 1999 than in 1979. What does date is the depth of the implementation: overdone scanlines and flicker read as 2015-era shader play, while the sober variant (chamfer, amber, labels) holds.

platforms.web: Very well within reach: clip-path chamfers, repeating linear gradients and corner brackets are cheap and tokenizable -- only the sweep layer should be dropped on weak devices.
platforms.mobile: The chamfer can be rebuilt exactly in Compose as a CutCornerShape (a rare case of genuine cross-platform coverage), but the wide caps and the dense labels have to be cut back considerably on small screens.
platforms.desktop: Its natural home -- Tauri windows with a housing metaphor, dense tool and monitoring surfaces, plenty of horizontal room for the wide type.

verdict: Of the three styles in this family the only serious candidate -- but not as a full build. What really carries here are four tokenizable decisions: the chamfered corner instead of a radius (identically reproducible in Compose as CutCornerShape), corner brackets as focus markers, monospace for everything measurable, and a single warm signal color. Those four run across Tailwind, Tauri and Compose with nothing lost and add up to a signature nobody else has. The complete amber CRT housing, by contrast, is too loud and too tiring for many small everyday apps and is not viable without a light mode -- it fits a dev or monitoring tool, not a balance or writing app. Recommendation: strip the style for parts, do not adopt it.
tip: Let the technical labels display something real. As soon as 'CH-7' is actually a channel number, 'REC 0032' a real counter and '01/02/03' the list index, the user reads the surface as an instrument -- if they are fantasy codes, they read as decoration and the whole style tips into cosplay. Second point: never chamfer all four corners, only two diagonally opposite ones. Four chamfered corners make an octagon and look decorative; two make a directed component.

finder.signature: Corners are chamfered by 20px instead of rounded -- only two, diagonally opposite; frames are brackets.
